subject: digital-design

questions.content: What does UI stand for?
questions.explanation: The user interface is what the user sees and interacts with: buttons, menus, text and images.

questions.content: What does UX stand for?
questions.explanation: UX is how a person feels and performs when using a product, including how easy it is to use.

questions.content: Which feature makes text easier to read?
options: Strong contrast between text and background
questions.explanation: High contrast helps readability, particularly for users with low vision.

questions.content: What is 'navigation' in an app?
options: The way users move between screens and find content
questions.explanation: Clear navigation, such as menus and back buttons, helps users find things.

questions.content: Why do designers use consistent buttons and icons across an app?
options: It makes the app load slower
Users learn the pattern once and can predict what things do
questions.explanation: Consistency reduces the effort of learning and avoids confusion.

questions.content: A user taps 'Submit' and nothing visible happens, so they tap it five times. Which design principle is missing?
options: Feedback showing the action was received
questions.explanation: Systems should give clear feedback such as a message or loading indicator.

questions.content: A form deletes an account with one tap and no warning. Which improvement is best?
options: Remove all text from the page
Make the delete button red only
Add a confirmation message before deleting
questions.explanation: Error prevention is an important usability principle: confirm destructive actions.

questions.content: Which choice best supports accessibility for users who cannot see images?
options: Adding descriptive alternative text (alt text) to images
questions.explanation: Screen readers read alt text aloud, so the meaning of the image is not lost.

questions.content: In an A/B test, version A gets 12 sign-ups from 200 visitors and version B gets 18 sign-ups from 200 visitors. What are the conversion rates?
questions.explanation: 12 ÷ 200 = 6%. 18 ÷ 200 = 9%. Version B performed better.

questions.content: Which layout is best for a thumb-operated phone app?
options: Important buttons large and within easy reach at the lower part of the screen
Tiny links at the top corners
questions.explanation: Large, well-spaced touch targets reduce mistakes.

questions.content: Why is it poor design to use red and green alone to show 'error' and 'success'?
options: Red and green are not allowed
Users with colour-vision deficiency may not see the difference
questions.explanation: Add icons or words so meaning does not rely only on colour.

questions.content: Which statement describes 'white space' in a layout?
options: A wasted area that must be filled
Empty space that separates items and makes the screen easier to scan
questions.explanation: White space (negative space) improves readability and focus.

questions.content: A usability test finds 6 of 10 participants cannot find the settings page. What is the best conclusion?
options: The navigation to settings needs redesign
questions.explanation: If most users fail at a task, the design is likely the problem, not the users.

questions.content: A designer reduces the number of taps to book a ticket from 6 to 4. Assuming each tap takes 2 seconds, what is the time saved per booking?
questions.explanation: Taps saved = 2. 2 × 2 seconds = 4 seconds.

questions.content: Two checkout designs were tested with 50 users each. Design 1: 40 completed. Design 2: 45 completed. What is the difference in completion rate?
questions.explanation: Design 1 is 80% and Design 2 is 90%. The difference is 10 percentage points.

questions.content: A designer adds 15 menu options to the home screen of an app 'so users have choice'. What is the most likely UX problem?
options: The app will use less data
Too many options make it harder and slower to choose
Users will read more slowly in dark mode
questions.explanation: Too many choices cause overload. Grouping and prioritising options improves usability.

questions.content: Which approach best balances a visually rich design with accessibility?
options: Use attractive images but provide alt text, sufficient contrast and keyboard-friendly controls
Hide the menu to look cleaner
questions.explanation: Good design meets both aesthetic and accessibility needs.

questions.content: A user-centred designer finds that older users cannot read 12 pixel text. What should they do?
options: Increase text size and test again with older users
questions.explanation: User-centred design adapts to users and tests the change.

note:
## UI and UX
The **user interface (UI)** is everything the user sees and touches: layouts, buttons, menus, icons, text, colours and images. The **user experience (UX)** is the overall feeling and effectiveness of using the product. A beautiful interface can still have poor UX if people cannot complete tasks. Good designers think about both, always starting with the needs of the target audience from Criterion A.

## Core design principles
- **Consistency**: use the same patterns for buttons, icons, colours and positions, so users can predict what happens.
- **Feedback**: show the user that an action worked, for example a loading spinner, a tick or a message.
- **Clear navigation**: users should always know where they are and how to get back. Menus should be simple and logically grouped.
- **Hierarchy**: size, colour and position show what is most important. Headings are bigger than body text.
- **White space**: empty areas separate content and make screens easy to scan.
- **Error prevention**: warn before destructive actions, such as deleting an account, and validate input.
- **Simplicity**: too many options slow people down. Group, prioritise and hide advanced features.

## Accessibility
Good products work for as many people as possible. Examples:
- **Contrast** between text and background. Light grey text on white is hard to read.
- **Alt text** on images so screen readers can describe them.
- **Not relying on colour alone**, since some people have colour-vision deficiency. Add words or icons.
- **Text that can be resized** and large touch targets for people with limited dexterity.
- **Captions** for video and **keyboard** access for people who cannot use a mouse.

## Colour, fonts and layout
Choose a colour palette that fits the audience and purpose and keep it consistent. Limit the number of fonts, usually to two. Align items on a grid. Group related items together (proximity). On mobile, place important controls within thumb reach and use large touch targets.

## Testing a UX
**Usability testing** watches real users complete set tasks. Measure the time taken, number of errors and number who succeed. An **A/B test** compares two versions. Example: version A gets 12 sign-ups from 200 visitors (6%) and version B gets 18 from 200 (9%), so B is better. When comparing percentages, say percentage points for the difference: 9% − 6% = 3 percentage points.

## Worked example
Design 1: 40 of 50 users complete checkout, which is 80%. Design 2: 45 of 50, which is 90%. The difference is 10 percentage points. Design 2 meets a 90% criterion and design 1 does not.

## How this is examined
Scenarios present a screen or short description and ask you to identify the principle broken, suggest the best improvement, interpret simple test data, or evaluate whether a design is accessible. Command terms: identify, suggest, justify, evaluate.

## Common mistakes
- Using decoration that distracts from the task.
- Hiding key functions in unclear icons.
- Testing only with the designer's friends.
- Saying a design is "user-friendly" without evidence.

Exam tip: Name the principle and then give a specific change. Example: "Add a confirmation message before deleting, to prevent accidental loss of data."

flashcards.back: User interface: the visible parts a user interacts with, such as buttons, menus and layout.
User experience: how easy, efficient and pleasant a product is to use.
Using the same patterns throughout a product so users can predict what things do.
A visible response to an action, such as a message, tick or loading icon.
Designing so people with different abilities can use the product, e.g. alt text and good contrast.
A written description of an image for screen readers.
Empty space that separates content and improves readability.
Watching users complete tasks to find problems in a design.
Comparing two versions of a design to see which performs better.

subject: digital-design

questions.content: Which language gives a web page its structure and content?
questions.explanation: HTML marks up headings, paragraphs, images and links. CSS styles them.

questions.content: Which language is mainly used to style a web page (colours, fonts, layout)?
questions.explanation: CSS controls the presentation of HTML elements.

questions.content: What does the 's' in https mean?
options: The site is stored on a school server
The connection is secure and encrypted
The site is for students only
questions.explanation: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server, protecting information such as passwords.

questions.content: What is a URL?
options: The web address of a page
questions.explanation: A URL such as https://example.com/page identifies the location of a resource.

questions.content: What does a responsive website do?
options: Adjusts its layout to fit different screen sizes
questions.explanation: Responsive design lets the same site work on phones, tablets and computers.

questions.content: Which HTML tag creates a hyperlink?
questions.explanation: The anchor tag with an href attribute links to another page. displays an image.

questions.content: Which code adds an image with alternative text?
questions.explanation: needs src for the file and alt for the description.

questions.content: What is the main difference between a web app and a native app?
options: Web apps cannot use the internet
A web app runs in a browser, but a native app is installed for a specific operating system
Native apps are written in HTML only
questions.explanation: Native apps are installed from a store. Web apps are accessed through a browser.

questions.content: A page includes a 2 MB image and loads on a connection of 8 megabits per second. About how long does that image take to download (1 byte = 8 bits)?
questions.explanation: 2 MB = 16 megabits. 16 ÷ 8 = 2 seconds.

questions.content: Why do designers compress images for websites?
options: To reduce load time and data use
questions.explanation: Smaller files load faster, which helps users on slow connections or limited data.

questions.content: Which is the best use of a site map in planning?
options: Showing how pages connect so navigation is logical
questions.explanation: A site map is a plan of pages and links, and helps design navigation.

questions.content: What does the client–server model mean?
options: A client such as a browser asks a server for pages or data, and the server responds
A server is the same as a screen
questions.explanation: The browser requests resources and the server sends them back.

questions.content: A mobile website's menu is hidden behind a three-line icon on small screens. What is the design technique?
options: Responsive design with a collapsible menu
questions.explanation: Responsive layouts change on small screens. The 'hamburger' icon saves space.

questions.content: A shop website works on a desktop but text overflows on a phone. Which CSS idea best fixes it?
options: Use flexible layouts and media queries for small screens
questions.explanation: Media queries and flexible units let the layout adapt. Fixed widths cause overflow.

questions.content: A designer wants search engines to understand a page. Which action best supports this?
options: Hiding text in the background colour
Using only images for all text
Using clear headings, descriptive page titles and alt text
questions.explanation: Search engines read structure and text. Meaningful headings and titles help both people and search tools.

questions.content: An app stores user scores in a database on a server. A user is offline. Which design best supports this?
options: Save scores locally and sync them when the connection returns
Ask the user to move to another country
questions.explanation: Offline support stores data on the device and syncs later, improving usability.

questions.content: A website asks users to enter their email on a page that starts with http:// not https://. What is the main risk?
options: Data could be intercepted because it is not encrypted
questions.explanation: Without HTTPS, data travels unencrypted and could be read by others on the network.

questions.content: A designer must choose between a web app and a native app for a school club with students using many different devices. Which is the best reason to choose a web app?
options: It works in browsers on all devices without separate versions for each system
questions.explanation: A single web app reaches many devices. Native apps may offer better performance but require separate versions.

note:
## How the web works A **website** is a collection of linked pages stored on a **server**. Your **browser** (the client) sends a request using a **URL**, and the server sends back files. **HTTPS** encrypts the connection, which protects data such as passwords. This is the **client–server model**. ## The three core languages - **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) gives structure and content: headings (

), paragraphs (

), links (), images () and lists. - **CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) controls appearance: colours, fonts, spacing and layout. - **JavaScript** adds behaviour: menus that open, form checks, animations and updating content without reloading. Example: shows an image and gives screen readers a description. ## Planning a site or app Use a **site map** to show pages and how they connect. Use **wireframes** for each page. Plan the navigation so key pages are only a few clicks away. Keep a consistent header, menu and footer. These support Criterion B. ## Responsive design People use phones, tablets and computers. **Responsive design** makes the layout adjust. Techniques include flexible grids, images that scale and **media queries** that change the layout at certain widths. On small screens menus often collapse into a three-line "hamburger" icon. A mobile-first approach designs for the smallest screen first. ## Web apps and native apps A **web app** runs in a browser and works on many devices. A **native app** is installed for a specific system (such as iOS or Android) and can use device features like the camera more directly, but needs separate versions. Choose based on the audience, devices and features needed. ## Performance Pages should load quickly. Large images are the most common problem. Compress images and use the right size. Download time = file size in bits ÷ speed in bits per second. A 2 MB image is 16 megabits, so on an 8 megabit-per-second connection it takes 16 ÷ 8 = 2 seconds. Remember that 1 byte = 8 bits. ## Databases and data Many sites and apps store data in a **database** on a server: user accounts, scores and products. For offline use, an app can store data locally and sync later. ## Security basics Use HTTPS, validate user input, use strong passwords and ask only for the data you really need. ## Search visibility Clear headings, meaningful page titles and alt text help people and search engines understand a page. ## How this is examined Scenarios involve a school or business website or app. Questions ask you to identify the role of HTML, CSS or JavaScript, choose responsive features, calculate a download time, or compare web and native apps for a given audience. ## Common mistakes - Mixing up the jobs of HTML and CSS. - Forgetting alt text. - Using fixed widths that break on phones. - Confusing bits and bytes. Exam tip: For web-versus-native questions, link your choice to the audience and devices given in the scenario.

flashcards.back: Markup language that gives a web page its structure and content.
Language that styles a web page: colours, fonts, spacing and layout.
Programming language that adds behaviour and interactivity to web pages.
Secure version of HTTP that encrypts data between browser and server.
A client (browser) requests resources and a server responds.
Layout that adapts to different screen sizes using flexible grids and media queries.
Web apps run in a browser on many devices. Native apps are installed for a specific operating system.
A diagram of pages and links used to plan website navigation.
File size in bits ÷ speed in bits per second. 1 byte = 8 bits.

subject: digital-design

questions.content: Which type of graphic is made of tiny coloured squares called pixels?
questions.explanation: Raster images are grids of pixels. Vector graphics use mathematical shapes.

questions.content: Which type of graphic stays sharp when enlarged to any size?
questions.explanation: Vector graphics are defined by shapes and paths, so they scale without losing quality.

questions.content: What does RGB stand for?
questions.explanation: Screens create colours by mixing red, green and blue light.

questions.content: Which file format is commonly used for photographs with small file sizes?
questions.explanation: JPEG uses lossy compression, which is good for photos.

questions.content: What does 'frame rate' mean in video?
options: The number of images shown per second
The size of the sound file
questions.explanation: Frame rate is measured in frames per second (fps).

questions.content: A video is 10 seconds long and runs at 24 frames per second. How many frames does it have?
A logo must be used on a business card and a billboard. Which format is best?
questions.explanation: Vector scales to any size without becoming pixelated.

questions.content: Which statement about lossy compression is correct?
options: It reduces file size by permanently removing some data
questions.explanation: Lossy formats (JPEG, MP3) discard some detail. Lossless formats (PNG) keep all data.

questions.content: An image is 1920 × 1080 pixels. How many pixels does it contain?
Which format supports a transparent background for a logo on a web page?
questions.explanation: PNG supports transparency and lossless compression. JPEG does not support transparency.

questions.content: A designer resizes a 400 × 300 pixel image to 1200 × 900 pixels. What is likely to happen?
options: The image looks blurry or pixelated
questions.explanation: Enlarging a raster image stretches the existing pixels and loses sharpness.

questions.content: Which action is cropping?
options: Making the file a different type
Removing unwanted outer parts of an image
questions.explanation: Cropping cuts away edges to improve composition.

questions.content: A design must keep a 16:9 ratio. The width is 1280 pixels. What height is needed?
An image file is 6 MB and, after compression, is 1.5 MB. What is the percentage reduction?
questions.explanation: The reduction is 6 − 1.5 = 4.5 MB. 4.5 ÷ 6 × 100 = 75%.

questions.content: An uncompressed image is 800 × 600 pixels at 3 bytes per pixel. What is its size in bytes?
A website needs a quick-loading banner showing a photo. Which choice is most suitable?
options: A JPEG compressed to suit screen size
questions.explanation: A compressed JPEG gives acceptable quality with small size. Large files slow loading.

questions.content: A poster designer uses an image copied from a website with no permission or credit. Which is the main issue?
options: The image has too many pixels
Copyright infringement and a failure to acknowledge the creator
The image has the wrong colour model
questions.explanation: Respecting copyright and giving credit are essential. Use licensed, free-to-use or self-created media.

questions.content: A stereo audio clip of 10 seconds uses 44 100 samples per second, 16 bits per sample and 2 channels. What is its uncompressed size in bytes?
questions.explanation: 44 100 × 16 × 2 × 10 = 14 112 000 bits. Divide by 8 to get 1 764 000 bytes.

note:
## Raster and vector graphics
**Raster (bitmap) images** are grids of tiny squares called **pixels**, each with its own colour. Photographs are raster. When you enlarge a raster image, the pixels stretch and the image becomes blurry. **Vector graphics** use mathematical shapes, lines and curves, so they can be scaled to any size without losing quality. They are ideal for logos, icons and illustrations. Common formats: JPEG, PNG and GIF are raster. SVG is vector.

## Image file formats
- **JPEG**: good for photographs, small files, uses lossy compression, no transparency.
- **PNG**: lossless, supports transparency, good for logos and screenshots.
- **GIF**: up to 256 colours, supports simple animation.
- **SVG**: vector format for scalable graphics on the web.

**Lossy compression** removes some data permanently to make files smaller. **Lossless compression** keeps all data, so the original can be restored.

## Colour
Screens use the **RGB** model, mixing red, green and blue light. Printers use **CMYK** inks (cyan, magenta, yellow, key/black). Web colours are often written as hex codes such as #FF0000 for red. Colour choices should suit the audience and keep text readable.

## Resolution and size
**Resolution** is the number of pixels. An image 1920 × 1080 has 1920 × 1080 = 2 073 600 pixels. File size (uncompressed) = pixels × bytes per pixel. For 800 × 600 at 3 bytes per pixel: 480 000 × 3 = 1 440 000 bytes. **Aspect ratio** is the ratio of width to height. For 16:9 with width 1280, height = 1280 ÷ 16 × 9 = 720.

## Editing techniques
Cropping removes unwanted edges. Resizing changes dimensions (keep the aspect ratio to avoid stretching). Layers let you edit parts separately. Adjusting brightness and contrast improves the image. Always keep an original copy.

## Video and audio
Video is a series of still images called **frames** shown at a **frame rate** in frames per second. 24 fps for 10 seconds is 240 frames. Audio is **sampled**: the sample rate (samples per second), bit depth (bits per sample) and number of channels all affect quality and size. Size in bytes = rate × bits × channels × seconds ÷ 8. Formats such as MP3 use lossy compression.

## Percentage reduction
A 6 MB file compressed to 1.5 MB has been reduced by 4.5 MB. 4.5 ÷ 6 × 100 = 75%.

## Legal and ethical use
Respect **copyright** and licences, such as free-to-use or licences requiring credit. Create your own media or give clear credit. Do not edit images to mislead people.

## How this is examined
Typical items give a media context, such as an advert or a school video, and ask you to choose the right format, calculate pixel counts or file sizes, find a percentage reduction or identify the legal issue.

## Common mistakes
- Enlarging a small raster image and expecting it to stay sharp.
- Using JPEG where transparency is needed.
- Forgetting to divide by 8 to convert bits to bytes.
- Using other people's images without permission.

Exam tip: In calculation questions, write the formula first, substitute the numbers, then state the unit.

flashcards.back: Made of pixels. Loses quality when enlarged. Photographs are raster.
Made of mathematical shapes. Scales to any size without losing quality.
Lossy compression permanently removes data. Lossless keeps all data so the original can be restored.
JPEG: photos. PNG: lossless with transparency. GIF: 256 colours and simple animation. SVG: vector.
RGB (light) is for screens. CMYK (ink) is for printing.
The number of pixels in an image, such as 1920 × 1080.
Pixels × bytes per pixel. 24-bit colour is 3 bytes per pixel.
The number of video frames shown per second (fps).
The ratio of width to height, for example 16:9.
